subject: biology
topicDisplay: Theme B · Organisms & Ecosystems (Gas Exchange, Transport, Adaptation, Niches)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Effective gas-exchange surfaces such as alveoli are:
options: Large in area, thin, moist and well ventilated
questions.explain: These features maximise the diffusion gradient and rate.

questions.q: Ventilation of the lungs maintains:
options: Steep concentration gradients for O2 and CO2
questions.explain: Refreshing alveolar air keeps diffusion rapid.

questions.q: In a leaf, gases are exchanged with the air mainly through the:
questions.explain: Guard cells open and close stomata to control gas exchange.

questions.q: Insects deliver oxygen directly to tissues using:
questions.explain: The tracheal system carries air directly to cells.

questions.q: Vessels that carry blood away from the heart at high pressure are:
questions.explain: Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand high pressure.

questions.q: Capillaries are adapted for exchange because they:
options: Have thin (one-cell-thick) walls and a large surface area
questions.explain: Thin walls and large area allow rapid exchange with tissues.

questions.q: In double circulation, blood passes through the heart:
questions.explain: Separate pulmonary and systemic circuits maintain pressure and oxygenation.

questions.q: Water rises up the xylem mainly by:
questions.explain: Evaporation from leaves creates tension pulling a cohesive water column upward.

questions.q: Phloem transports sugars:
questions.explain: Translocation moves organic compounds from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits).

questions.q: In respiring tissues (low oxygen), haemoglobin tends to:
questions.explain: At low partial pressure of oxygen, haemoglobin unloads oxygen to tissues.

questions.q: A cactus (xerophyte) is adapted to dry conditions by having:
options: Spines/reduced leaves and a thick cuticle
questions.explain: These reduce transpiration and help store water.

questions.q: Small ears and thick fur in Arctic mammals are adaptations that:
options: Reduce heat loss in the cold
questions.explain: Reduced extremities and insulation conserve body heat.

questions.q: An ecological niche is best described as:
options: An organism's role and interactions, including how it obtains resources
questions.explain: The niche includes habitat, feeding and interactions, not just location.

questions.q: The competitive exclusion principle states that:
options: Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche indefinitely
questions.explain: One species will outcompete the other if they use identical limiting resources.

questions.q: Two warbler species feeding in different parts of the same tree show:
questions.explain: Dividing resources lets similar species coexist.

questions.q: An organism that obtains carbon by ingesting other organisms is a:
questions.explain: Heterotrophs consume organic matter; autotrophs synthesise their own.

questions.q: Which change would increase the rate of gas exchange across a surface?
questions.explain: Rate rises with steeper gradient, larger area and shorter distance.

questions.q: Valves are found in veins to:
questions.explain: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backward.

questions.q: Adaptations arise in a population through:
questions.explain: Heritable variations that improve survival and reproduction become more common over time.

questions.q: The mode of nutrition of an organism (autotroph or heterotroph) is part of its:
questions.explain: How an organism obtains energy and nutrients is a key aspect of its niche.
